newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan has few options to respond to U.S. warning.
newsitem.headline: Japan has few options to respond to U.S. warning.

text.p: The United States appears to have warned Japan against solving its economic woes by boosting exports, but economists say that for now policy makers in Tokyo have left themselves few other options.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin referred to Japan's multitude of troubles on Saturday, telling a news conference in Berlin: "They clearly have difficult issues to deal with."
"These concerns merit a fair bit of attention going forward," said Rubin, who spoke after a Group of Seven (G7) financial leaders' meeting that called for currency stability.

Behind such comments lurk concerns that Japan's bulky trade surplus might again start to balloon, that its fiscal tightening could stifle recovery, and that its shaky banking system could see defaults that might damage the world economy.
Some economists said Rubin was merely putting Japan on notice that the world is watching to see if Tokyo's bet that its recovery can survive belt-tightening would pay off.

Others, however, said he was signalling irritation at Tokyo's determination to forge ahead with plans to raise taxes in its budget for the year from April 1, a move many economists say could pour cold water on Japan's slowly improving economy.

"The U.S. has been doing all it can to help the Japanese economy by letting the dollar go up and the yen go down," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities in Tokyo. "What has Japan done? Tighten fiscal policy again."
"I think the U.S. is saying 'we've done all we can...while Japan has made a negative contribution'," Jerram added.
Washington has already subtly altered its strong dollar stance, which had helped push the greenback up more than 50 percent from its post-war low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.
On Friday, Rubin jolted currency markets with remarks seen as hinting he might not be unhappy with some weakening of the U.S. currency -- or at least that he sought no further gains.
The G7 nations called on Saturday for currency stability, saying their currencies were no longer greatly misaligned.

The yen's fall has already boosted Japanese exports, which the weaker currency makes more price-competitive abroad, and Japan's trade surplus is expected to stop falling later this year after four years of decline.

That competitive threat due to the yen's drop has sparked an outcry in the United States from American carmakers and their workers. "There is obviously a lot of pressure within the U.S. in terms of the automakers, their unions and lobbyists complaining about the dollar's strength," Jerram said.

At the same time, however, Washington is worried that Japan's sluggish growth will exacerbate the woes of its financial system, a development which could have negative fallout for U.S. markets and its economy.
Jitters over the health of Japan's banking sector have resurfaced this year and been a key factor behind sagging Tokyo share prices.
But analysts see little chance that Japan will ease its tight fiscal stance, while interest rates are already at rock-bottom levels and so can provide no further relief.
"If you take away the weak yen, the outlook is very bleak indeed," ING Baring's Jerram said.

That means that the best Tokyo can do may be to forge ahead with promised deregulation of its economy -- measures that spell pain for protected sectors but which proponents argue will ultimately stimulate higher growth.
"Traditional fiscal or monetary policy to stimulate domestic demand will not be forthcoming," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute.
"So what Japan has to do is deregulate. That will take time to have an effect, but it's really the only option."
